messages.author: 99feee15920ab812
messages.subject: g(o)
parts:
Dear List,

We have been distance sampling badgers (Meles meles) using spotlights,
in Gloucestershire, U.K. The area is made up of mixed woodland/scrub and
open agricultural land. We found it impossible to survey for badgers in
woodland and so concentrated all our efforts on open land. From radio
tracking studies we found that badgers spend on average 48.5% of their
time on open land. From bait marking studies we know the delineation of
badger territories and therefore the area of open land and woodland for
each territory.

Our question concerns the calculation of abundance. As far as we know
this can be done either of two ways:

1. You use the 0.485 figure as a multiplier of g(0). This then
calculates what the density would be if all badgers were on the open
land at once. i.e. the abundance of the population of interest. One
obvious advantage of this method is that DISTANCE utilises the variance
associated with the radio tracking fixes, when calculating the
confidence of the density estimate.

2. You calculate the abundance of badgers on open land only, assuming
g(0)=1 (which is a fair assumption) and then use the radio tracking data
to estimate the number of badgers that weren't on the open land.
Obviously the sum of the two equals the total abundance within those
social groups.

Both these methods produce the same estimate of abundance (not
surprisingly). However, the first method seems a bit contrived (i.e.
artificially adjusting the g(0)), although it has the advantage of
including the variance associated with the radio tracking multiplier.
The second method seems more intuitive but, including the associated
variance is beyond us! Can it be done? Are both these methods equally
valid?

Any advice would be great.

Cheers,

Tim.

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: g(o)
parts:
Tim, Distance allows multipliers for various reasons. There is no need to
regard it as an estimate of g(0). The multiplier (first) method is more
appropriate, because your second method doesn't estimate the number in
woodland directly. Rather, you still base estimation on the multiplier,
to estimate the woodland component. Thus variance estimation is more
naturally handled through the multiplier method. See pp57-8 and 182 of
the 2001 book.

Steve
